blocks.text: Chapter 2.
The Associative Machine
Second night with Kahneman, friend — and tonight I'm going to do something to you. Ready? Read these two words:
Bananas. Vomit.

There — it already happened. In the last two seconds your face flickered with a trace of disgust. Your memory quietly fetched sickness. For the next few minutes you'll recognize words like "nausea" a beat faster — and you'll feel, absurdly, a little cooler toward bananas. Nobody asserted anything, friend. Two words sat side by side... and your mind built a little causal story linking them, printed it, and filed it — all without asking you.

That's the machine we're touring tonight: associative activation. Your memory is a vast web of linked ideas — concepts, emotions, even bodily states — and touching one node sends current spreading through its neighbors, and their neighbors, fast, parallel, and almost entirely invisible. You're conscious of only a sliver of what your own mind just stirred. Two properties matter, friend. The cascade is coherence-seeking — it weaves whatever lights up into the most sensible story it can, quietly suppressing alternatives. And it runs both ways: ideas move the body, and the body moves ideas — hold a pencil crosswise in your teeth, forcing a smile, and cartoons get funnier; nod along while listening, and you agree more.

Now the strangest chapter of this science, told honestly. In John Bargh's famous experiment, students who unscrambled sentences seeded with Florida, forgetful, bald, wrinkle then walked measurably slower down the hallway — primed with old age, they became old for a minute. Money-primed people grew more independent but more selfish, even placing chairs farther apart. People who'd just recalled a shameful act craved cleansing products — with eerie specificity, friend: those who lied on the phone preferred mouthwash; those who lied by email preferred soap. But here's the part I insist on telling you fireside, because it honors this book's own sermon: many of these dazzling results later collapsed. Big, careful, preregistered replications found little or nothing behind the Florida effect and money priming — and Kahneman, to his lasting credit, publicly conceded he'd put too much faith in small studies, and urged the field to clean house. The man who taught the world about overconfidence caught it in himself and said so out loud. The safe residue is modest but real: the associative web exists, and context genuinely colors judgment — but trivial cues do not routinely steer big behaviors.

Pause and guess: And yet one humble experiment in this family keeps its charm. A university office kitchen ran an honesty box — pay for your own tea and coffee, unsupervised. Researchers changed ONE thing about the kitchen, week by week, and in alternating weeks the box collected nearly THREE TIMES more money. What was the change?
Ready? Here is what happened.

A poster of eyes. Some weeks the sheet above the box showed flowers; other weeks, a pair of watching eyes — and under the gaze of printed eyes on paper, contributions nearly tripled, friend. Nobody believed the poster could see them. System 1 doesn't care what you believe — being watched is one of its oldest alarm bells, and a symbol is enough to ring it. Now connect this to the machine's quality signal: cognitive ease. At every moment System 1 tracks whether processing flows smoothly or labors — but it reports everything as ONE undifferentiated feeling. So the causes blur, friend: whatever is easy — repeated, clearly printed, familiar, met in a good mood — feels true, likable, and safe, regardless of why it was easy. See a made-up name like David Stenbill once on a list, and days later it feels familiar — and familiarity gets misread as fame. Repeat any phrase often enough and the illusion of truth kicks in. Rhymes are judged more insightful — "woes unite foes" beats its plain paraphrase. Stocks with pronounceable tickers outperform tongue-twisters in their first week. And Zajonc's mere exposure effect is the deepest cut: meaningless Turkish-like words, printed repeatedly in campus newspapers with no explanation, came to be liked — an effect that works even when stimuli flash too fast to consciously see... even in chicks, friend, played tones before hatching. The biology is ancient: what has recurred without harming you is probably safe. Repetition is a salesman, and it's whispering to you all day.
The world model that writes itself

Beneath the associations, friend, System 1 maintains a running model of your normal world — and measures every event against it. Surprise is just the model crying "violation!" And the model updates with unnerving speed. Kahneman twice bumped into the same acquaintance, Jon, in wildly improbable places — and by the second time, meeting Jon in odd places had become its own little category; a third time would have felt normal. One diner wincing at the soup is a surprise. When a second diner winces... the two events reach back in time and explain each other.

This is norm theory: we judge events not against forecasts made in advance, but against norms recruited after the fact. It's why "the large mouse climbed over the trunk of the tiny elephant" parses instantly — each noun drags its own private scale of normal along with it. It's why, in a story where Jane loses her wallet in a crowded New York street, listeners later swear the word "pickpocket" was said — it never was; the norm supplied it.
Pause and guess: Let me spring the classic on you, friend, exactly as the researchers do. Quick — answer from the gut: How many animals of each kind did Moses take into the ark?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Did you say two? Almost everyone does... and it was Noah, friend — Moses never had an ark. That's the Moses illusion: Moses is normal enough in a biblical sentence that System 1 raises no alarm, and the question sails through unchecked. Your world-model checks for weirdness, not truth. And the machine does one more trick automatically: it sees causes. Albert Michotte showed that when one shape on a screen slides into another and the second instantly moves, observers don't infer launching — they perceive it, as directly as color, though nothing exists but sequenced motion. Heider and Simmel animated two triangles and a circle — and viewers can't help seeing a bully, a defender, a frightened victim; six-month-old infants already parse such scenes as agents acting. Paul Bloom argues this born readiness to see minds everywhere is a root of religion itself. Here's the toll on the bridge, friend: causal stories come free, statistics cost effort. So when randomness wiggles — a hot streak, a bad quarter, three coincidences in a row — System 1 hands you a beautiful story about why... and never mentions that noise needs no author. Hold that thought; it becomes the villain of several coming nights.
Before you go

So: your mind is an association engine — two adjacent words write causal stories without permission; the body and mind prime each other both ways; the dazzling social-priming results mostly failed replication, and Kahneman's public self-correction is the book's own lesson wearing a lab coat; easy feels true — repetition, rhyme, and clean fonts are salesmen; the world-model normalizes fast, checks for weirdness rather than truth (poor Moses), and sees causes and intentions the way it sees color. This week, friend: when a claim just feels true, ask whether you've ever seen evidence — or merely heard it repeated. And before one big judgment, audit what you read, watched, and felt in the hour before.

Tomorrow, the machine's most dangerous habit gets a name you'll never forget. Why did Kahneman coin the ugly acronym WYSIATI — what you see is all there is — and how does your mind answer hard questions by secretly swapping in easy ones... without telling you the question changed? Next time: jumping to conclusions.
Key takeaways
Associative activation: one idea lights a spreading, coherence-seeking web of ideas, emotions, and bodily states — mostly below awareness, and it runs both ways (ideomotor effect).
The famous social-priming results (Florida effect, money priming) largely failed preregistered replication — Kahneman publicly conceded overconfidence; keep the modest core: context colors judgment.
Watching-eyes posters nearly tripled honesty-box takings — System 1 responds to symbols of being watched regardless of belief.
Cognitive ease is one blurred feeling: easy = familiar = true = good — repetition breeds belief (illusion of truth), rhymes persuade, pronounceable tickers win week one.
Norm theory: the world-model checks weirdness, not truth — hence "two" for Moses's ark and the never-spoken "pickpocket" remembered as said.
We perceive causes and intentions directly (Michotte's launching, Heider-Simmel's bullying triangle) — causal stories are free, statistics are expensive, so noise gets an author it never had.
